Assessing Generalisation in AI-Generated Music Detection

Angelos-Nikolaos Kanatas1, David López-Ayala1, Pablo Zinemanas2, Martín Rocamora1, Xavier Serra1, Dmitry Bogdanov1

1Music Technology Group, Universitat Pompeu Fabra, Barcelona
2BMAT Licensing, Barcelona

Paper arXiv Data Code
AbstractKey resultsFamily exclusionsGenerators, all families presentArtifactNetWithheld generatorsDecoder classesCross-corpus pairsStrictly unseenGenerators per pairMUSIC8KHuman poolsThresholdsInventoryReproducibility

Abstract

AI-generated music detectors can perform well on familiar data, but evaluations on new collections often change both generators and human-made music, making failures of generalisation difficult to interpret. We compare spectral-artifact detectors, frozen-encoder readouts and retrained baselines. To distinguish missing generator families from reduced training data, we compare each family exclusion with an equally sized training pool that retains the family, using identical test recordings. Across six family-exclusion comparisons, spectral-template detectors incur larger mean AUROC losses than frozen-encoder readouts, with substantial variation across families. In contrast, with generated recordings fixed, AUROC varies more across human-made collections for the evaluated encoder-based methods than for spectral detectors. A learned combination of encoder and spectral scores achieves .928 mean AUROC across nine training–test corpus pairs, exceeding its components and retrained baselines. Source-calibrated thresholds can still produce excessive false alarms after transfer. For a 5% false-alarm target, recalibration on 200 target human-made recordings yields 4.3% mean false alarms and 76.1% detection for the learned combination. Generator coverage, sensitivity to human-made collections and threshold transfer therefore require separate evaluation.

This page disaggregates the paper's two tables: each family exclusion, each generator, each training–test pair, each human-made pool, and both decision thresholds. Every value is recomputed from the saved per-recording scores of the fitted detectors; nothing was refitted for this page, and the rows printed in the paper are reproduced before any table is written (S13, Reproducibility). AUROC throughout, higher is better; a loss is AUROC with a family removed minus AUROC under the size-matched control. AB is ArtifactBench, FMC is FakeMusicCaps, M8K is MUSIC8K; detector names follow the paper's tables. Figures and tables are numbered S1–S13 so that the paper can cite them.

Key results

Four views that the paper's tables compress into single numbers. Colours follow the paper's figure: fusion, spectral templates, fingerprint, trajectory readout, mean and attention pooling, retrained baselines.

How to read

  • Table 1 protocol. Pooled training on the other two target collections plus SONICS. A family is removed from fitting and development wherever it occurs; the control keeps it but subsamples generated recordings to the removal count within each collection and split. Both arms score the same target recordings of that family against the same target humans.
  • Six primary comparisons (Suno, Udio in ArtifactBench and Echoes; MusicGen in ArtifactBench and FakeMusicCaps) were selected first; the seven extension comparisons (Stable Audio, AudioLDM, DiffRhythm) were added afterwards.
  • Table 2 protocol. One training collection, one test collection; nine pairs enter the summary (SONICS targets excluded: bandwidth alone separates the classes there). MUSIC8K averages four source-trained models against the same 1,102 FakeMusicCaps humans.
  • Per-generator AUROC is that generator's recordings against all human-made recordings of the same target. Slices under 40 recordings are marked with a dagger; they are descriptive.

Scope and limits

  • Repeated control draws or repeated detector fits: every comparison rests on one fit per arm and one control draw. The intervals shown resample recordings with the fitted models fixed.
  • MusicDET and CoMoE were not run on the seven extension comparisons (MusicDET fits human-made recordings only, so removing a generated family cannot change it). Per-generator results for the released ArtifactNet exist only where per-recording scores exist (ArtifactBench, Echoes, MUSIC8K).
  • An acoustic duplicate audit across collections; leakage control is by recorded identity, prompt and reference groups.
  • Any per-recording mechanism attribution. Decoder classes are annotations from public specifications; proprietary services are marked undisclosed.

S1. Family exclusions, every comparison, every detector

Table S1. Removed minus size-matched control AUROC on the withheld family, per comparison. Base is mean AUROC on the full target test set with no family excluded. Hover a cell for the removed and control values; switch the metric to see them directly. Intervals are 95% recording-bootstrap intervals conditional on the fitted models (2,000 draws), available for the nine systems the bootstrap covered.

lossgainn = generated recordings of the withheld family in the target; humans: ArtifactBench 860, Echoes 59, FakeMusicCaps 1,102

Source: the pooled-training scores behind the paper's Table 1, including the seven additional comparisons and the parameter-matched single-support control. The printed rows are reproduced in Table S13a.

S2. Generators with every family present

Table S2. Pooled-base models (no family excluded), one target collection at a time: AUROC of each generator's recordings against all humans of that collection. Rows carry the family and the annotated decoder class. This is the descriptive map of where each detector succeeds and fails before any exclusion.

Source: the same pooled-training scores with no family excluded.

S3. Released ArtifactNet by generator, at its native input rate

Table S3. The released ArtifactNet build, scored by us with native input where the collection is distributed above 16 kHz, on the paired subsets where both the native and the 16 kHz input exist. Its training mix contains several of the evaluated families, so it is printed in the paper and not ranked; this table shows where it succeeds and fails per generator.

S4. Withheld generators, version by version

Table S4. For one family exclusion, every generator of the withheld family in the target: AUROC with the family removed (large figure) and under the size-matched control (small figure). Provenance slices of one brand behave differently; the paper's Suno and Udio version readings come from this table.

MusicDET and CoMoE were run on the six primary comparisons only; every other detector covers all thirteen.

S5. Decoder classes on the pooled bases

Table S5. Target humans against the target recordings of one annotated decoder class, per target and detector, with every family in the pool. Classes absent from a pool are the weakest for every detector (Riffusion is excluded from all pools; Echoes' loop-recombination service has no relative anywhere), so absence and mechanism are not separated here.

Decoder classes are annotations from public specifications, marked verified, likely or unknown per generator in Table S12; proprietary services are undisclosed.

S6. Cross-corpus transfer, pair by pair

Table S6. Train on one collection, test on another. The nine pairs of the paper's summary are the four trainers against ArtifactBench, Echoes and FakeMusicCaps; SONICS-target cells are shown but flagged (bandwidth cue); MUSIC8K cells use the same FakeMusicCaps humans. Released checkpoints are evaluated from their own training pools. Switch to the carried false-alarm rate: the trainer's 5% human threshold moved unchanged to the target.

Source: the scores behind the paper's Table 2; the printed rows are reproduced in Table S13b. Carried false-alarm rates are those of the paper.

S7. Strictly unseen: brand and decoder class both absent from the training collection

Table S7a. Each cross-corpus cell's generated recordings are split by whether the trainer collection contained the generator's brand and whether it contained its decoder class. The strict subset has neither; the disclosed variant further drops proprietary generators whose class cannot be known. Means are over the nine summary pairs (three for released checkpoints); a subset needs at least 20 recordings to score.

S11. Decision thresholds, carried and recalibrated

Table S11. Six training-test pairs with at least 200 held-out target humans (Echoes targets excluded). Carried: the trainer's 5% order-statistic threshold applied unchanged. Recalibrated: the same rule on 200 target humans, which are then excluded from evaluation; both thresholds are evaluated on identical recordings within a system. Means balance trainers as in the paper's figure.

The trainer-balanced means are those of the paper's Figure 1.

S12. Generator inventory

Table S12. Every generated source in the four evaluation collections: recording count in the target set, the collection's own source label (for Echoes, the conditioning mode: TTA text-to-audio, ATA audio-to-audio), brand used for the overlap flags, annotated decoder class and the confidence of that annotation.

Counts are those of the evaluation sets; decoder classes come from public specifications.

S13. Reproducibility

All values on this page were recomputed from the saved per-recording scores of the detectors evaluated in the paper; no model was refitted for the page. As a check, the rows printed in the paper's two tables are reproduced from the same scores (Tables S13a and S13b).
